source_text: δέ, ἡ ἐξ ἀνάγκης βία μετὰ τοῦ προεπινοεῖσθαι τὴν βούλησιν καὶ πρὸ ἐκείνης τὴν νόησιν τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς ὑποστάσεως τῆς πάντῃ τε καὶ πάντως ἐχούσης συνυφεστὸς τὸ ἀπαύγασμα. 9.21 Πρὸς τούτῳ εἰ πιστεύουσι τὰ πάντα ἐκ τῆς βουλήσεως τοῦ πατρὸς διὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ γεγονέναι, οὐ προϋπάρχει ἡ βούλησις. ἀμήχανον γὰρ καὶ ἀδύνατον μὴ τὸν δημιουργὸν ὑφεστάναι καὶ μετέπειτα δεδόχθαι τὸ δι' αὐτοῦ δημιουργῆσαι. 9.22 Ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦτο ἀσυνεσίας μεστόν. εἰ γὰρ αὐτός φησιν· «ἐγώ εἰμι καὶ οὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι», πῶς ἡ ἀναλλοίωτος φύσις ἀλλοίωσιν ὑποσταίη κατὰ τὰς ὑποστάσεις μὴ ἐν ταυτότητι τῶν προσώπων ἑστῶσα, ἀλλὰ κινουμένη καὶ μεταπίπτουσα; 9.23 Ἔτι καὶ τοῦτο. εἰ ἀληθές, ὥσπερ οὖν ἀληθές, τό «ἅπερ ἂν ὁ πατὴρ ποιῇ, ταῦτα καὶ ὁ υἱὸς ὁμοίως ποιεῖ», ποιήσει καὶ ὁ υἱὸς ἄλλον υἱόν, ἵνα πάντα ὁμοίως τῷ πατρὶ ποιήσῃ. 9.24 εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐποίησεν οὐδὲ ποιεῖ, οὐκ ἔστιν κτίσμα οὐδ' ἡγεῖται αὐτοῦ πατρικὴ βούλησις. 9.25 Εἴποιμι καὶ ἕτερον· εἰ λέγει ὁ σωτήρ· «θέλημα τοῦ πέμψαντός με, ἵνα πᾶς ὁ θεωρῶν τὸν υἱὸν καὶ πιστεύων εἰς αὐτὸν ἔχῃ ζωὴν αἰώνιον», οὐκ ἐκ θελήματος ὁ υἱὸς, ἀλλ' ὁ θεωρῶν αὐτόν. 9.26 τὸ γὰρ θέλημα μετὰ τὸν υἱὸν κἀνταῦθα εὑρίσκεται. 9.27 Ἀπεώσαιτο δ' ἂν καθ' ὅλου τις θᾶττον αὐτῶν καὶ τουτονὶ τὸν λόγον οὐκ ἐκ μόνων τῶν προλεχθέντων, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ἐπαχθησομένων πρὸς ἡμῶν· τουτέστιν, εἴγε παραπλήσιον ἀντέρηται αὐτούς· «πότερον ποτὲ ὁ πατὴρ θελήσας ὑπάρχει ἢ οὔ;», τὰ ἴσα γὰρ ὧν ἐμελέτησαν ἀπαντήσει αὐτοῖς· πρὸς μὲν τὸ «οὐ θελήσας», ὅτι παρὰ σκοπὸν αὐτῷ συνέβη τὸ ὑφεστάναι, φύσεως ἀνάγκης εἰς τοῦτο αὐτὸν ἄκοντα περιτρεπούσης· πρὸς δὲ τὸ δεύτερον, ὅτι πρὸ τῆς θελήσεως οὐκ ἦν· ἀναχθήσεται γὰρ ἡ ὕπαρξις αὐτοῦ εἰς τὴν βούλησιν αὐτοῦ· δημιουργικῶς αὐτόν, κατὰ τὰς βαττολογίας αὐτῶν, εἰς ὑπόστασιν περιελαυνούσης. 9.28 Ὁμοίως καὶ ἄλλο, λέξει μόνον διαφέρον τοῦ πρὸ αὐτοῦ· «θελητῶς ὁ θεὸς ἀθάνατός ἐστιν καὶ ἀγαθὸς ἢ ἀνεθελήτως;» ἐπενεχθήσεται γὰρ τὰ αὐτά. 9.29 Κάλλιον δέ τις ποιήσει, εἰ συντόμως ἀποκρίνηται αὐτοῖς, μηδὲν ἐπισυμβαίνειν τῷ παντελείῳ θεῷ μηδέ τι ἀπολιμπάνειν αὐτόν· 9.30 καὶ ὥσπερ οὐ προηγεῖται τῆς πατρικῆς ὑπάρξεως καὶ ἀθανασίας καὶ ἀγαθότητος θέλημα, οὕτως οὐδὲ τῆς γεννήσεως· καὶ ἀπᾴδειν πάντα ὁπόσα τοιαῦτα τῆς περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνθυμήσεως· 9.31 περὶ δὲ τῶν κτιστῶν τὸν ∆αυῒδ ᾄδειν ἐν ριγʹ ψαλμῷ· 9.31 «ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ· καὶ ἐν τῇ γῇ, πάντα ὅσα ἐθέλησεν ἐποίησεν», καί «πάντα ἐν σοφίᾳ ἐποίησας», τουτέστιν ἐν τῷ υἱῷ, οὐχὶ δὲ ἐν θελήματι, 9.32 καὶ ἐν οβʹ ψαλμῷ· «ἐκράτησας τῆς χειρὸς τῆς δεξιᾶς μου, ἐν τῇ βουλῇ 5 σου ὡδήγησάς με καὶ μετὰ δόξης προσελάβου με», καὶ ἐν κθʹ· «ὅτι ὀργὴ ἐν τῷ θυμῷ αὐτοῦ καὶ ζωὴ ἐν τῷ θελήματι αὐτοῦ», καί ἐν· «κύριε, ἐν τῷ θελήματί σου παράσχου τῷ κάλλει μου δύναμιν», καὶ ἐν ιζʹ· «ῥύσεταί με, ὅτι ἠθέλησέν με». 9.33 Καὶ γὰρ ὃν τρόπον, ὑπάρχων ὁ πατὴρ ἀθάνατός τε καὶ ἀγαθός, βούλεται εἶναι ταῦτα καὶ βουλόμενός ἐστιν ταῦτα, οὐκ αἰτίαν, ἵν' οὕτω φράσω, τὴν βούλησιν ἔχων οὔτε μὴν ἀνεθελήτως ὤν· οὕτως οὐδὲ τοῦ γεννῆσαι ἡ βούλησις αἰτία. 9.34 περὶ ἡμᾶς δὲ τὸ τινὰ μὲν ἐκ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνεργείας, τινὰ δὲ ἐκ τοῦ ἐφ' ἡμῖν θελήματος ἔχειν· 9.35 καὶ γὰρ οὐ βουλήσει μὲν τῇ ἑαυτῶν, ἀλλὰ τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ κτώμεθα τὸ συνεστάναι ἐκ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος καὶ τὸ εἶναι λογικοί· 9.36 οἱ γὰρ οὔποτε ὄντες πῶς εἴχομεν βούλεσθαι ἢ μὴ βούλεσθαι; 9.37 προαιρέσει δὲ ἰδίᾳ ἔχομεν τὸ εἶναι καλοὺς ἢ κακούς, ἐπιστήμονάς τε κατ' ἐπιτηδειότητα ἢ ἀνεπιστήμονας κατὰ ῥαθυμίαν. 9.38 Ἐληλύθασιν δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ κεφάλαιον τοῦτο οὐκ ἀτρεκεῖ θεωρήματι παραδεχόμενοι τό «οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός, ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα», ἐπεὶ ἂν αὐτόθεν εἶχον τῆς ὀρθῆς πίστεως ἄγκυραν βεβαίαν. 9.39 νυνὶ δὲ φάσκουσιν, ὅτι τό «ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα» δείκνυσι κτίσμα τὸν υἱόν.
pass_a_gloss: [...but before not willing yet doing there goes] the force from necessity, together with the will being conceived beforehand, and before that the act of thinking, prior to the hypostasis of the Father, which in every way and altogether has the radiance subsisting with it. 9.21 In addition to this, if they believe all things to have come into being from the will of the Father through the Son, the will does not exist before. For it is unmanageable and impossible that the craftsman not subsist and afterwards it be resolved to craft through him. 9.22 But this too is full of senselessness. For if he himself says: 'I am and I have not been altered', how would the unalterable nature undergo alteration according to the hypostases, not standing in sameness of the persons, but moving and falling over to another state? 9.23 Further this too. If it is true, as indeed it is true, the [saying] 'whatever the Father does, these the Son also does likewise', the Son too will make another son, so that he may make all things likewise to the Father. 9.24 But if he did not make and does not make, he is not a thing made, nor does a paternal will go before him. 9.25 Let me say another thing too: if the Saviour says: 'will of the one who sent me, that everyone who beholds the Son and believes into him may have eternal life', not from will is the Son, but the one beholding him. 9.26 For the will is found after the Son here too. 9.27 And someone would thrust away more quickly and altogether this argument of theirs too, not only from the things said before but also from those to be brought on by us; that is, if he asks them in turn something similar: 'is the Father existing having willed or not?', for things equal to what they rehearsed will meet them: toward 'not having willed', that against his aim the subsisting happened to him, nature's necessity turning him unwilling into this; toward the second, that before the willing he was not; for his existence will be led up into his will, [the will] driving him around into subsistence in a craftsman's way, according to their babblings. 9.28 Likewise also another, differing only in wording from the one before it: 'is God immortal and good willingly or unwillingly?' For the same things will be brought on. 9.29 But someone will do better if he answers them briefly that nothing happens in addition to the all-perfect God nor does anything leave him lacking; 9.30 and just as will does not go before the paternal existence and immortality and goodness, so neither the generation; and that all things of this sort are out of tune with the thinking about God; 9.31 and that about the created things David sings in the 113th psalm: 9.31 'our God in heaven; and in the earth, all things whatever he willed he made', and 'all things in wisdom you made', that is, in the Son, but not in will, 9.32 and in the 72nd psalm: 'you held my right hand, in your counsel you guided me, and with glory you took me to yourself', and in the 29th: 'because wrath in his anger and life in his will', and in [number missing]: 'Lord, in your will furnish strength to my beauty', and in the 17th: 'he will rescue me, because he willed me'. 9.33 For in the manner in which, the Father being immortal and good, he wills to be these things and willing is these things, not having the will as cause, so that I may phrase it thus, nor yet being unwillingly; so neither of the begetting is the will cause. 9.34 But about us [it is] to have some things from the working of God, and some from the will in our power; 9.35 for not by our own will but by that of God do we acquire the being composed from soul and body and the being rational; 9.36 for we who were not yet, how were we able to will or not to will? 9.37 But by our own choice we have the being good or bad, and knowing according to fitness or unknowing according to slackness. 9.38 And they have come to this head not with an exact contemplation accepting the [saying] 'this is my Son the beloved, in whom I was well pleased', since they would have had from it at once a firm anchor of the correct faith. 9.39 But now they assert that the 'in whom I was well pleased' shows the Son a thing made.
pass_b_english: … the force that comes of necessity. And with it comes the notion that the will, and before the will the act of thought, can be conceived as prior to the hypostasis of the Father, a hypostasis that in every respect and at every point has the radiance subsisting together with it.

Besides this, if they believe that all things came into being from the will of the Father through the Son, then the will does not exist beforehand. For it is unworkable and impossible that the Creator should not yet subsist and that afterwards the decision should be taken to create through him.

But this too is full of folly. For if he himself says, “I am, and I have not been changed” (Malachi 3:6), how could the unchangeable nature undergo change with respect to the hypostases, not standing firm in the sameness of the persons but moving and shifting?

And there is this as well. If it is true, as indeed it is true, that “whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise” (John 5:19), then the Son too will make another son, so that he may do all things just as the Father does. But if he has not made one and does not make one, then he is not a creature, and no fatherly will goes before him.

Let me say something more. If the Saviour says, “This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who beholds the Son and believes in him should have eternal life” (John 6:40), then it is not the Son who comes from will, but the one who beholds him. For here too the will is found after the Son.

One could thrust away this argument of theirs too, altogether and more quickly, not only by what has been said already but also by what we shall now bring against them. That is, suppose one puts to them in turn a like question: “Does the Father exist because he willed it, or not?” For the very same things they have rehearsed will meet them in return. To “not because he willed it” the answer will be that his subsisting befell him against his purpose, since a necessity of nature turned him, unwilling, to this. To the second, the answer will be that before the willing he was not. For his existence will be traced back to his will, and the will, as their babbling has it, drives him into subsistence as a craftsman makes a thing.
Likewise with another question, which differs from the one before it only in wording: “Is God immortal and good by willing it, or without willing it?” For the same things will be brought against it.

But one will do better to answer them briefly: nothing comes upon the all-perfect God as an addition, nor does anything fall short in him. And just as no will goes before the Father’s existence, his immortality and his goodness, so none goes before the generation either. All such notions are out of tune with right thinking about God.

It is concerning created things that David sings in Psalm 115, “Our God is in heaven; and on the earth he has made all things whatever he willed” (Psalm 115:3), and “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 104:24), that is, in the Son, and not in a will. So too in Psalm 73: “You took hold of my right hand; you guided me by your counsel, and you received me with glory” (Psalm 73:23-24). And in Psalm 30: “For wrath is in his anger, and life in his will” (Psalm 30:5), and in [the same psalm]: “Lord, by your will grant strength to my beauty” (Psalm 30:7). And in Psalm 18: “He will rescue me, because he willed me” (Psalm 18:19).

For in the same way that the Father, being immortal and good, wills to be these things and, willing, is these things, yet does not have his will as their cause (if I may put it so), nor is he these things without willing them, so the will is not the cause of his begetting either.

With us, however, some things we have from the working of God and others from the will that lies in our own power. For it is not by our own will but by God’s that we come to be composed of soul and body and to be rational. How could we, who did not yet exist, will or not will? But by our own choice we are good or bad, and knowledgeable by applying ourselves or ignorant through sloth.

They have come to this head of their argument by taking up, without an accurate understanding, the words “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Had they understood them, they would have had from those very words a firm anchor of the right faith. But as it is, they claim that “in whom I am well pleased” shows the Son to be a creature.

be out of tune with, disagree

choices.issue: Old draft garbled, mis-referenced and split
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English printed edition numbers 9.21-9.28 in the reading text; broke the question of 9.28 across two paragraphs ('God wills the immortal...' / 'Is it also good or unwilling?'); made 9.24 'nor is his paternal will reckoned as such' (ἡγεῖται: no paternal will goes before him); 9.26 'with the Son' (μετὰ τὸν υἱόν: after the Son); 9.30 'one can sing all such things' (ἀπᾴδειν: they are out of tune); garbled 9.33; and made 9.38 'not being unsettled in their theory' (οὐκ ἀτρεκεῖ θεωρήματι: without an accurate understanding). Psalm sources were wrong: 'Psalm 104:24 with a trembling psalm' for LXX Psalm 113, 'Psalm 119' for LXX 72, '1 Chronicles' for LXX 29, '2 Samuel' for the unnumbered psalm, 'Psalm 118' for LXX 17. Psalm 73:24 widened to 73:23-24; 'cf. John 5:19' and 'Matt 3:17' written as full references.

choices.english: … the force that comes of necessity.
choices.why: The section opens inside the sentence begun in 9.20 (willing is preceded by desire, not-willing-yet-doing by compulsion). Only the words this section holds are translated, with a leading ellipsis.

choices.term: μετὰ τοῦ προεπινοεῖσθαι τὴν βούλησιν καὶ πρὸ ἐκείνης τὴν νόησιν τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς ὑποστάσεως
choices.english: the will, and before the will the act of thought, can be conceived as prior to the hypostasis of the Father
choices.why: The genitive τῆς … ὑποστάσεως depends on προ- in προεπινοεῖσθαι: the absurdity is that will and thought would be conceived before the Father's own hypostasis.
Didymus numbers the Psalms by the Greek Bible (113, 72, 29, 17); converted to English numbers and checked by verse text.
Bracketed supplement for a lacuna: the copy-text has 'in' with the psalm number missing. The verse quoted is in the same psalm as the one before (LXX 29:8, English Psalm 30:7).
The '5' is a printed line number in the copy-text (page debris); skipped.
The copy-text reads the imperative παράσχου; the Septuagint has παρέσχου (you furnished). Translated as printed; see problems.
Didymus reads 'wisdom' as the Son and denies that creation in wisdom means creation in a will; kept literal.
Didymus' scornful word for the Arian argument; kept, not softened.

choices.english: as a craftsman makes a thing
choices.why: Adverb from δημιουργός: the will would bring the Father into being the way a maker produces a product.
ἐπιτηδειότης (fitness) stands against ῥαθυμία (sloth) under προαίρεσις (choice), so it names a chosen readiness or application, not an inborn aptitude.

choices.english: Had they understood them, they would have had from those very words
choices.why: The unreal condition is implied by ἐπεὶ ἄν; English states it so the sentence reads aloud. No new claim.
The Arian thesis Didymus rejects: the Son as a thing made.
